crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practices and tools that let another person rerun a quantitative analysis and get the same results, from data loading through to final figures and tables.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language means a person types a question such as 'What were sales by region last quarter?' and a system translates it into a query against a database or dataset, then returns an answer, often as a table or chart.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the systems and practices used to run heavy analytical and machine learning workloads over datasets that an organization holds under its own rules, such as university research archives, hospital records, government registers, and corporate transaction logs.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers using AI assistants to draft, refactor, explain, and test code for statistical analysis, data cleaning, modeling, and visualization.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its question with the data it expects to gather.

sections.body: Quantitative analysis with AI covers the practical work of turning data into defensible results, and reproducible work covers the habits that let someone else rerun those results. In practice, AI now helps write analysis code, suggests statistical tests, drafts notebook cells, and translates a plain language question into a query or script. It also helps plan a study before any data exists, by simulating what a design might detect. The work is less about new statistics and more about speed and error checking across the whole analysis chain. A researcher still decides what the question means and whether the answer is credible.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Reproducibility itself is largely solved as a technical matter, since notebooks, environment files, and version control are mature and widely used. What is not solved is the gap between a working notebook on one machine and a working pipeline on another, especially when institutional data cannot leave its host. AI assistance with statistical code is useful but unreliable at the edges, and it can produce plausible code that runs without error while answering the wrong question. Large scale compute on protected data remains the hardest part, because access controls, cost, and queue times shape what is even testable. Testing a design before collection is promising but depends on assumptions the researcher supplies, so it is a planning aid rather than a guarantee.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section moves from the mechanics of rerunning work to the questions that come before it. Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines is the foundation, covering how to structure code and environments so results can be checked, and it is the page to read first if your analysis already exists. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language sits on top of that, showing how natural language requests become queries and what gets lost in translation. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data addresses the setting where the data cannot move, which changes every other decision in the section. Writing Statistical Code with AI focuses on the code layer itself, including how to test what a model generates before trusting it. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection closes the loop by moving upstream, using simulation to check whether a planned study can answer its own question. Read together they form a sequence from planning to execution to verification.
